common_name: Ironbark Pumpkin (Australian Heirloom Dark-Green Storage Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after all danger of frost; needs a long, warm season and ample vine room.

directions: Ironbark is an Australian heirloom dating to the Victorian gold-rush era of the 1850s, prized for its thick, hard, dark blue-green bumpy rind that is notoriously difficult to cut, which gives the variety its name. The round, flattened, deeply ribbed fruits weigh roughly 5-18 lbs and are packed with dense, dry, bright orange flesh that is sweet and excellent baked or roasted. The exceptionally hard rind gives Ironbark outstanding storage life, often keeping well past other winter squash. It remains a popular home-garden variety in Australia but is still uncommon in North America.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; tolerates heat and dry conditions better than many C. maxima types.

directions: Iran is a rare heirloom winter squash originally collected in northeastern Iran in the 1940s and preserved in the USDA seed bank before being reintroduced to home gardeners by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Long, vigorous, heat- and drought-tolerant vines produce large round-oval fruits with silvery-green skin mottled in pale orange. The orange flesh is sweet and can be baked, roasted, or pureed like other Cucurbita maxima squash. Its notable heat and drought tolerance make it a useful choice for hot, dry-summer gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; give vines room to run.

directions: Candystick Dessert is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by independent plant breeders Carol Deppe and Nate France in Corvallis, Oregon, and released through the Open Source Seed Initiative to keep it permanently free of patent restriction. Fruits are tan with green stripes and notably larger than standard delicata, averaging 2-3 lbs, with thick flesh and a smaller seed cavity. The dense flesh has an intensely sweet, dessert-like flavor that many compare to Medjool dates, and it holds its sweetness in storage longer than most delicata types. It is widely adapted, grown successfully from the Pacific Northwest to the Southeast and Northeast.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm; as a Cucurbita moschata type it tolerates heat and humidity well.

directions: Shishigatani is a traditional Kyoto heirloom squash and one of the certified Kyo-yasai heritage vegetables, developed in the 19th century from chrysanthemum-type pumpkins brought south from Tsugaru in northern Japan. Fruits develop a distinctive bumpy, waisted, gourd-like snowman shape rather than the rounded form of typical kabocha. The squash carries deep cultural significance in Kyoto, where Anraku-ji Temple holds an annual squash-blessing ceremony each summer, and it is traditionally simmered in shojin ryori Buddhist vegetarian cooking. It remains a rare specialty variety outside Japan.

common_name: Nanticoke Squash (Native American Heirloom Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; allow ample room for vigorous vines.

directions: Nanticoke is an heirloom landrace squash grown for generations by the Nanticoke people of the Delmarva Peninsula, Delaware and the Eastern Shore of Maryland, and is one of the few surviving Native American winter squash lines from the Eastern Woodlands. Fruits have a mottled, speckled green rind that cures to a hard protective shell suited to long winter storage. The flesh is rich golden-orange, dense, fine-grained, and sweet, good for baking and roasting. It is maintained today primarily by seed-preservation and Indigenous seed-rematriation projects.
sources: The Seed Farm at Princeton University

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; vigorous moschata vines need room to spread.

directions: Canada Crookneck traces to the Iroquois Nations and was first offered commercially in the 1830s, making it one of the oldest named squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. The bottle-shaped, curved-neck fruits are relatively small, typically 2-4 lbs, with a warty tan rind and sweet, fine-grained orange flesh. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving for its history and flavor. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has notably better resistance to squash vine borer than C. pepo or C. maxima types.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Magdalena Big Cheese Pumpkin (Sonoran Desert Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; this heat-tolerant moschata type suits long, hot growing seasons.

directions: Magdalena Big Cheese is a Sonoran Desert heirloom pumpkin with roots in Sonora, Mexico, grown by Southwestern gardeners and maintained by regional seed-saving organizations. It produces large, flattened, wheel-shaped fruits weighing 15-30 lbs with light orange, ribbed skin resembling a wheel of cheese. The dense, fine-grained flesh is richly sweet and well suited to soups, purees, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries useful resistance to squash vine borer and tolerates heat well, fitting arid Southwestern growing conditions.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; vines show strong tolerance to squash bugs and common cucurbit diseases.

directions: Thai Kang Kob was brought from Thailand to the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds' Andrew Kaiser in 2006 and has since become popular for its productivity and disease resistance. The heavily ribbed, warted fruits are sea-green at harvest and age to chestnut brown in storage, weighing about 6-8 lbs. The deep orange flesh is sweet and fragrant, traditionally used in Thai coconut curries, soups, and stir-fries, as well as the custard-filled dessert sangkaya. Vines tolerate squash bugs and common cucurbit pests and diseases better than many winter squash.

common_name: Green Delicious Squash (1903 Heirloom, Parent of Golden Delicious)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; allow vines ample room to run.

directions: Green Delicious was introduced in 1903 by James J.H. Gregory and Sons of Marblehead, Massachusetts, and was described in the historical reference The Vegetables of New York as among the finest-flavored of all squash. Its thick, hard green rind protects dense, orange, fine-grained flesh with an exceptionally sweet, dry texture prized for pies and baking. It later served as a parent, crossed with Boston Marrow, in the 1926 development of the now much more widely grown Golden Delicious squash by Gill Brothers Seed Company. Green Delicious survives today mainly through heirloom seed preservationists.
sources: U.P. Hedrick, The Vegetables of New York

common_name: Warsaw Pasta Squash (Polish Bush Spaghetti Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost; compact bush habit suits smaller gardens.

directions: Warsaw Pasta is a spaghetti-type squash from Poland, offered in the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Compact, disease-resistant bush plants bear pale yellow, elongated-oval fruits weighing about 2-5 lbs. When cooked, the fine-grained flesh separates into tender, mild-flavored strands like traditional spaghetti squash, and the bush habit makes it a good choice for gardeners with limited vine space.
sources: ECHO Book and Gift Store and Nursery

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm; harvest when the rind is firm and the stem has turned brown.

directions: Crespo is one of the traditional zapallo squash of the Andes, grown in Peru and Bolivia and sold widely in local markets there before being introduced to North American gardeners through Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. As a Cucurbita maxima type it produces large fruits valued for their dense, sweet, gourmet-quality flesh, well suited to roasting, soups, and traditional Andean dishes. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the stem has browned, then cure for improved storage and flavor.
